title: Guest isolation and scaling drift — on-call chronicle and runbook notes
content:
Summary:

This is an on-call chronicle from the Feb 16–17 dedicated pool degradation incident that primarily affected tenant isolation and autoscaler behavior. The root problem appears to be a subtle interaction between (a) a busy, long-lived tenant that holds large KV caches + pinned kernels, and (b) a mis-tuned autoscaler threshold for ephemeral burst queues. Net: several nodes became GPU-saturated while cluster autoscaler declared them healthy and therefore did not evict the noisy tenants quickly enough.

Impact:
- Duration: ~4.5 hours of elevated p99 latency for dedicated-gpu pool (10:22–14:52 UTC on 2025-02-16)
- Affected customers: 3 Dedicated tenants (internal latency SLO alerts) + 7 hosted fallbacks saw increased cold-starts
- Observable: GPU memory oscillation, NVML power/SM load at ~95% on 4 nodes, but host-level CPU and network not pegged

How we detected it:
- 10:20 — Pager triggered: dedicated-gpu p99 > 450ms (alerts channel)
- Oncall jumped in Slack channel and ran initial checklists from existing SRE playbook
- 10:25 — Quick dashboards: per-node GPU memory and nvml_utilization showed sustained high usage; node-level metrics (kubelet readiness) still OK
- 10:35 — Confirmed multiple long-running processes (tenant pods with pinned quantized model variants) holding large KV caches (see pod mem info below)

Immediate mitigation we used:
- 10:40 — Thawed aggressive eviction policy: manually cordon + drain on two worst nodes (kubectl cordon/drain with --ignore-daemonsets) to trigger pod rescheduling across pool
- 11:05 — Applied temporary weight-based traffic reroute to fallback tier for affected tenant via routing-layer flag (route=dedicated->fallback) to reduce new requests
- 11:20 — Rebalanced caches: restarted 3 pods after notifying tenant owners (caused brief cold-starts but freed GPU memory)
- 12:00 — Autoscaler policy tweak: lowered the scale-up threshold from 80% avg GPU mem to 65% over 2min for burst queues (manual override) — careful: experimental and must be reverted after incident

What we observed while mitigating:
- Draining nodes did reduce per-node peak utilization but caused short-term increase in scheduling pressure elsewhere
- One node repeatedly received evicted pods that rehydrated large caches and hit same limits; suggests affinity/anti-affinity rules are too permissive for these tenants
- The autoscaler’s decision signals are based on pod cpu/ram, not GPU memory for this pool; this blind spot allowed autoscaler to under-react

Data & commands used during triage (notes to future on-call):
- List offending pods: kubectl -n dedicated-gpu-prod get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.containerStatuses[0].state.runningSince
- Per-pod GPU usage (via host): ssh gpu-node-XX and run: sudo nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o DT or nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,used_gpu_memory --format=csv
- Inspect process inside pod: kubectl exec -n dedicated-gpu-prod <pod> -- bash -c "ps aux | grep model_server" then use nvprof / dcgmi as available
- Check autoscaler decisions: kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/cluster-autoscaler --since=6h | grep -i "scale up\|scale down"
- Check routing layer: curl -sS https://console.redwood.internal/api/routing/status?pool=dedicated-gpu-prod

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Noisy tenant with long-lived KV caches pins quantized kernels and GPU memory — causes sustained memory pressure that isn't visible to autoscaler (high confidence after nvml evidence)
2) Autoscaler metrics don't account for GPU occupancy (moderate confidence; confirmed by reviewing autoscaler config)
3) Scheduling/affinity allowed co-location of multiple heavy tenants on same node (lower confidence but supported by pod placement logs)

Root cause summary (short):
- A mix of tenant workload characteristics that were not covered by existing placement and scaling heuristics: heavy GPU memory + long-lived caches + autoscaler blind to GPU memory. This allowed the cluster to appear healthy while GPUs were saturated.

Proposed immediate runbook changes (to add to existing playbooks):
- Add a quick-check at top of dedicated-capacity runbook: check NVML metrics for node-level GPU memory + util (command examples above).
- Add explicit autoscaler health probe: include a GPU memory metric (via node-exporter GPU exporter) as a soft signal for scale-up recommendations.
- Emergency isolation step: script (one-liners) to apply a temporary PodDisruptionBudget override + `kubectl label` to move offending pods into a dedicated anti-affinity group and then drain nodes.
- Add a 'noisy-tenant' label and an automated small-cache eviction endpoint for model server so we can request cache trim via API instead of restarting pod.

Longer-term engineering tasks (action items):
- ENG-RED-421 (sched): Enforce stronger anti-affinity for tenants whose pods have annotation `redwood/kv-cache=true` — schedule across distinct GPUs/nodes.
- ENG-RED-429 (autoscale): Extend cluster-autoscaler integration to accept GPU memory pressure from node-exporter-gpu and treat it as a scale-up hint.
- OPS-RED-433 (routing): Add adaptive routing fallback thresholds so the routing layer reduces traffic to dedicated pool when global p99 crosses threshold for X minutes.
- SRE docs: update dedicated-pool runbook with the above quick checks and include the exact commands and Slack channel templates.

Action items tracked (owners + ETA):
- Maya (me): Draft runbook edits + add NVML quick-check snippet — ETA 2025-03-05
- Arjun: Small API endpoint on model_server to drop KV cache (PR 412 linked) — ETA 2025-03-12
- Theo: Autoscaler proto to include GPU memory metric (spike experiment) — ETA 2025-04-01
- Lena: Post-incident customer comms draft (for impacted tenants) — ETA 2025-03-04

Post-incident notes / lessons learned (freeform):
- Need to treat GPU memory analogous to host memory in autoscaling heuristics; CPU-only signals are insufficient for inference-heavy workloads.
- Long-lived tenant processes are predictable sources of friction; add detection for pods that rehydrate large caches on restart (track startup memory ramp).
- Consider introducing a tenant-grade policy: tenants that opt into higher isolation (billed) get hard anti-colocation and guaranteed node reservations.

Runbook snippet (to paste into playbook):
- Detect: run nvidia-smi on suspected nodes, grep for high used_gpu_memory percentage > 80% for > 2min.
- Isolate: kubectl label pod <pod> redwood=noisy-tenant=1; kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force
- Short-term reroute: use routing API: POST /internal/routing/modify {"pool":"dedicated-gpu-prod","action":"reroute","target":"fallback","reason":"noisy-tenant"}
- Rebalance: restart model_server for cache-trim after owner consent: kubectl rollout restart deployment/<deployment> -n dedicated-gpu-prod

Open questions (still unresolved):
- Is there a way to instrument the model server to report approximate KV cache footprint before restart? (short-term: add logs)
- Are there tenant-level quotas we can apply that auto-throttle connections rather than rely on cluster autoscaler?

Appendix: raw snippets captured during incident
- Example pod mem: "pod-quantizer-7f9c  gpu_mem_used: 10.7GB  gpu_mem_total: 16GB  cache_size: ~8.4GB"
- Autoscaler excerpt: "NoScale: nodes stable; cpu usage 35%; memory 42% -> no action" (but note: GPU memory missing)
- Slack excerpt (sanitized): "@oncall: seeing p99 spike, PV mounts OK, nvidia util 98% on node-7; initiating cordon"

Notes to self: keep this short and actionable; scrub tenant IDs before sharing externally; file follow-up PRs for runbook insertion.

End of chronicle.
